title: Interned at Compiegne and Creteil; bugler and orchestra
summary: After a week at Compiegne he was transferred to a camp with a thirty-piece amateur orchestra and negotiated eating with the kitchen staff in return for blowing four daily bugle calls.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: At Creteil. They first sent us to Compiegne. And I stayed at Compiegne, say about a week. Because, there was another Allied camp, where they had a group of about thirty amateur musicians, and as you know, the only type of music we could play then was light music and symphonies and things. That was the only music that was permitted by the Germans. And they had in this camp, they had about a thirty-piece orchestra, but they claim that they didn't have satisfaction with the brass or the trumpets, 'cause they were more or less amateurs, you see.
And the person who was leading the band, he knew me, and he knew of my internment, and he asked the Germans to give me a transfer.

I was then transferred to this camp in Creully, where I stayed. I had no problem 'cause I told the Germans when I got to the camp and saw what they were dishing out for food, I said, "I couldn't blow my instrument on that."

So at the abouer -- an abouer is a German office, And the officer, he was a man of a certain age, he was certainly of the old stock, 1914 stock. He was awfully nice. He said, "Look, what can I do for you, Mr. Briggs?" I said, "Well, look, I do not want work in the kitchen, but I'd like to eat with the kitchen folks. He said, "Is that all you'd like Mr. Briggs?" I said, "Yes." He said, "Well, you know, you have quite a lot of work anyhow, 'cause you have to -- now, in order -- I'll do that for you, but I would like you to blow the 'Reveille' in the morning, and at breakfast, and for a check-up
and everything --" Four calls a day.
"That's fine," I said, "But how do I know that it works." He said, "In ten minutes it will be on the board." (Laughter).
And I was committed to the kitchen staff, as I said, just for eating, you see. And that was pretty good. 'Cause they worked. They worked hard and they deserved to have what they had.
And I guess that's one of the reasons why I'm here today. Of course, my wife came to see me whenever she could, and she brought me a hot meal, whenever she could, as well.
